newsitem.title: INDIA: More Kashmir violence as India condemns killings.
newsitem.headline: More Kashmir violence as India condemns killings.

text.p: Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Monday condemned the killings of seven Hindus in the troubled Himalayan region of Kashmir.

"I wish to emphasise that the perpetrators of this act of terror shall not escape the consequences of their horrible crime," Deve Gowda said in a statement issued before he left for a three-day visit to Russia.

"Their masters abroad, who aid and abet cross-border terrorism, should understand that the entire Indian nation stands together in the defence of the territorial integrity and secular unity of the country," Deve Gowda said.

Deve Gowda's remarks coincided with a sudden upsurge of violence in the disputed province that also saw six separatist Moslem guerrillas and one Indian soldier killed in incidents on Sunday and Monday.
Jammu and Kashmir is India's only Moslem-majority province and has been wracked by an insurgency by Moslems seperatists.
The bloodshed began on Friday when police said 15 gunmen encircled Hindu homes in Sangrampur village, 20 km (13 miles) southwest of Srinagar, the summer capital of India's Jammu and Kashmir state.
The unidentified gunmen forced eight men outside, saying security officials wanted to see them, and later shot them outside the village, police said. One survived.

Police said the incident was the worst violence against Hindus since September, when India held the first provincial elections in the state since 1987. There was no claim of responsibility for the attack, but violence against Hindus in Kashmir is usually blamed on Islamic separatists.

Police also said one Indian soldier and four separatist guerrillas died in a 12-hour gun battle on Sunday on Srinagar's outskirts. On Monday, two leaders of the Tehrik-ul-Mujahideen guerrilla group were killed in a shootout with counter-insurgency forces in central Srinagar.
"In the exchange of fire...the self-styled supreme commander of the Tehrik-ul-Mujahideen, Abdul Rehman Molvi, was killed," the police spokesman said.
He said Bilal Ahmed, another leader of the same group, was also killed in the shooting.
The Tehrik-ul-Mujahedin is one of at least 12 groups fighting Indian rule in Jammu and Kashmir.
Deve Gowda's statement came just four days before bitter enemies India and Pakistan are to resume talks broken off three years ago and which are likely to include the acrimonious subject of Kashmir.
Pakistan, which controls one-third of the province, has fought two wars with India over Kashmir since the two nations gained independence from Britain in 1947.
Pakistan denies Indian charges that it arms and trains Kashmiri separatist guerrillas.

Referring to the September elections, won by a pro-India party, Deve Gowda said: "The full restoration of democratic government in Jammu and Kashmir has opened a new chapter and has decisively defeated the designs of the terrorists and their masters abroad."

Kashmir's leading separatist organization, the All-Parties' Hurriyat (freedom) Conference, which comprises some 30 religious and political groups, condemned Friday's killings as the work of anti-separatist forces bent on defaming the Moslem rebels.
Insurgency-related violence has claimed more than 20,000 lives.
